[THOUGHT] Clinical reasoning:

This is a classic presentation of a giant invasive pituitary tumor producing very high prolactin. Key points: progressive headaches and progressive bilateral visual loss with profound bitemporal field defects and optic atrophy indicate long-standing suprasellar mass compressing the chiasm. MRI shows a >5 cm bilobed sellar/suprasellar mass with cavernous sinus invasion, carotid encasement, extension into sphenoid and posterior fossa regions — imaging most consistent with a large pituitary macroadenoma (“snowman” configuration). The serum prolactin is 8,094 ng/mL (normal 4–15 ng/mL). Mild–moderate hyperprolactinemia can be from stalk compression, but the degree here is far above levels typically seen with stalk effect (usually <200 ng/mL) and is strongly supportive of a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma (giant prolactinoma). The homogenous, hypo-enhancing bilobed appearance and invasive behavior fit a macroadenoma; craniopharyngioma, meningioma, germ cell tumor, and metastasis are less likely given imaging and the extremely high prolactin. Pituitary carcinoma (malignant lactotroph tumor) is extremely rare and usually requires metastatic disease to define; invasive appearance alone does not establish carcinoma. Hook effect (falsely low prolactin) is the opposite problem and not relevant here because prolactin is very high. Overall the most likely diagnosis is a giant lactotroph (prolactin-secreting) pituitary macroadenoma; other possibilities include a nonfunctioning macroadenoma with stalk compression (less likely given level), invasive lactotroph carcinoma (rare), and other invasive sellar masses (craniopharyngioma, meningioma, metastasis) causing secondary hyperprolactinemia.
